opus-5.5.text:
I think SWE-bench is genuinely one of the better benchmarks out there, and a big part of that is that it's grounded in real work. These are actual GitHub issues from real open-source Python repositories, and the model has to produce a patch that makes the hidden tests pass. That's very different from something like HumanEval, where you're writing a self-contained function from a docstring. With SWE-bench you have to navigate an unfamiliar codebase, figure out where the problem actually lives, understand how the pieces fit together, and make a change that doesn't break everything else. That's much closer to what a software engineer does day to day.

That said, it definitely has limitations, and I'd be careful about treating it as a complete picture of software engineering. A few that come to mind:

First, it's all Python, and it's drawn from a fairly small set of popular repos. Those projects are well-structured, well-tested, and likely well-represented in training data, so it isn't fully representative of the messy internal codebases people work in at companies.

Second, the tasks are pretty well-scoped. You get an issue, and there's a specific fix that the tests check for. A lot of real engineering is upstream of that: working out what the requirements even are, talking to people, deciding what *should* be built, making architectural tradeoffs. SWE-bench doesn't really measure any of that.

Third, there's noise in the dataset itself. Some issues are underspecified, and some tests check implementation details that you couldn't reasonably infer from the issue. That's why SWE-bench Verified was valuable: having humans filter down to problems that are actually solvable made the numbers much more meaningful.

And finally, it's a pass/fail test-based metric, so it doesn't capture code quality, readability, or whether a human reviewer would actually want to merge the change. You can pass the tests with a pretty ugly patch.

So my overall take is that it's a really useful signal, especially for agentic capability: can the model use tools, explore an environment, and iterate toward a working solution? When we worked on our agent, a lot of the gains came from getting the scaffolding and tools right, letting the model run code, view files, and edit carefully, rather than from any clever prompting. But I'd see it as measuring one important slice of software engineering, not the whole job. As models saturate it, we'll need benchmarks that are longer-horizon, more ambiguous, and closer to real product work.

r001.rationale: It says SWE-bench is limited to Python and a fairly small set of popular repositories, making it less representative of internal company codebases.

r002.rationale: It describes the benchmark as using actual GitHub issues from real open-source repositories and says this resembles day-to-day engineering work.

r003.rationale: It contrasts SWE-bench’s codebase navigation and integration work with HumanEval’s self-contained function-writing task, then says SWE-bench is closer to day-to-day software engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I have kind of a love-hate relationship with SWE-bench. On the love side, it was a huge step forward. Before SWE-bench, most coding evals were basically HumanEval-style, write a function from a docstring, and that just has almost nothing to do with what a software engineer actually does all day. SWE-bench said, here's a real repository, here's a real GitHub issue, go fix it and make the hidden tests pass. That's directionally much closer to the job. It forced everyone to think about agents instead of single-shot completions, it forced tool use, navigating a codebase, running tests, iterating. That was a big deal, and I think it genuinely pushed the field in a good direction.

The hate side is that the moment a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes against, it starts to drift away from what it was measuring. A few specific issues. One, it's all Python, and it's heavily concentrated in a handful of repos like Django and sympy, so you're really measuring "how good are you at a particular flavor of mature Python open-source project." Two, the tasks are selected so that there's a clean, pre-existing test that flips from failing to passing. Real engineering work mostly isn't like that. The hard part is often figuring out what the right behavior even is, or writing the tests, or negotiating with the person who filed the issue about what they actually want. SWE-bench strips all of that out. Three, there's a contamination question. These are public repos with public fixes, and the models have almost certainly seen a lot of them in pretraining. Verified helped with quality, but it doesn't fully solve that.

And then the more subtle thing is what I'd call the agentic gap. Even when a model solves the task, the way it solved it matters. Did it write a sensible, minimal patch a reviewer would accept? Or did it bludgeon the tests into passing with something you'd never merge? The benchmark score doesn't distinguish those. When we look at real usage internally, the things that actually determine whether an engineer trusts the model are stuff like, does it know when to stop and ask, does it avoid breaking things three files away, does it clean up after itself. None of that shows up in a pass rate.

So the way I'd put it is, SWE-bench is a pretty good measure of a necessary capability. If you can't do well on it, you're definitely not a good software engineer. But doing well on it is nowhere near sufficient. We treat it as one signal among many, and honestly the signal I care most about now is just watching people use the model on their actual codebases for a week and seeing whether they keep using it. That's a much noisier eval, but it's the one that's actually hard to game.

r001.rationale: It says SWE-bench is all Python and concentrated in a handful of repositories, so it measures a narrow flavor of mature Python open-source work.

r002.rationale: It calls SWE-bench a major step forward because it asks models to fix real GitHub issues in real repositories, closer to the job.

r003.rationale: It contrasts HumanEval-style function writing from a docstring with what software engineers do day to day.

astra-6.text:
I think SWE-bench is useful because it’s grounded in real issues in real repositories. You have to understand an existing codebase, make a change, and get the tests to pass. That’s much closer to software engineering than solving a little standalone coding puzzle.

But it’s still a fairly narrow slice of the job. You’re handed an issue and there’s a way to evaluate whether you solved it. In practice, a lot of engineering is figuring out what the problem actually is, clarifying requirements, and deciding which tradeoffs to make. And passing the tests doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the solution is maintainable or fits the architecture.

So I’d treat it as a useful signal of an agent’s ability to fix well-defined problems in an existing codebase, rather than a complete measure of how much engineering work it can take off your plate.

r001.rationale: It calls SWE-bench a narrow slice of the job, but does not identify narrow repository coverage as the limitation.

r002.rationale: It values SWE-bench because it uses real issues in real repositories and requires working in an existing codebase.

r003.rationale: It says repository issue work is closer to software engineering than solving a standalone coding puzzle.

sol-6.1.text:
I think SWE-bench is a useful benchmark because it’s grounded in real issues in real repositories. You have to understand an existing codebase, figure out where the problem is, and make a change that passes tests. That captures an important part of software engineering.

But it’s a narrower task than the job itself. You’re given an issue and a way to evaluate the fix. In practice, a lot of the work is figuring out what to build, clarifying ambiguous requirements, and making tradeoffs that will matter months later. So I’d treat SWE-bench as evidence that a model is getting better at solving well-specified repository tasks, rather than a direct measure of how much of a software engineer’s job it can do.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench is narrower than the job itself and measures well-specified repository tasks, limiting how directly it represents a software engineer’s full work.

r002.rationale: It values SWE-bench because it is grounded in real issues in real repositories and requires understanding a codebase and fixing a problem.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish coding interview questions or puzzles from day-to-day software engineering work.
